title: The Blue Circle on the Seventh Purchase Order
teaser: Purchase prices were lower, stockouts were fewer, and sales were still rising, yet the warehouse kept filling with the same kind of cup. The problem was not that the buyer was doing something plainly wrong. It was which version of 'right' his rewards encouraged when he was the one holding the market information.
paragraphs: On Thursday morning, Chen Cheng counted the 137th wooden-handled thermal cup at the far end of the warehouse. Three months earlier there had been only 48. Yet that afternoon's monthly report looked good: sales were up 8 percent, average purchase prices were down 3 percent, and the three stores had fewer stockouts than before. She had to decide that day whether to keep the same purchasing rules for the next month. Luo Qi, the buyer, had not hidden anything, nor had he pushed unsellable stock into a forgotten corner. Customers were genuinely buying these cups every day.

Two years earlier, when Chen Cheng had only one store, she used to leave before dawn and buy stock herself at the wholesale market. After expanding to three stores, she handed purchasing to Luo Qi because he knew the stalls better, could distinguish return rates and supply reliability, and understood temporary discounts. Over the past year, the new products he selected had also performed noticeably better than the ones Chen Cheng chose remotely. She kept only a monthly sales target and paid him a bonus based on sales. The supplier of the wooden-handled cups gave a 12 percent discount for orders of 60 and reserved popular colors for larger buyers. Based on recent sales, 30 cups were enough to cover short-term demand, but 60 meant both a lower unit price and more stock on hand.

So Luo Qi repeatedly chose 60. From where he sat, the decision was sensible. His sales bonus benefited when more units were available to sell, lower purchase prices helped as well, and the cash tied up in extra inventory and the shelf space it occupied did not enter his bonus. The monthly report initially rewarded the same direction: higher sales, lower purchase prices. Only when several colors had gone six weeks without needing replenishment, while a full row of warehouse shelving was still occupied by old stock, did Chen Cheng see that the inventory capital and space she cared about were absent from Luo Qi's most immediate decision criteria.

At first, she did not change the bonus. She asked for photographs of the shelves, prices, and negotiation outcomes for every purchase. A month later, the group chat held more than two hundred extra photos, and full-case orders of 60 were still appearing. The photos could prove one quoted price, but they could not show which alternatives Luo Qi had rejected or recreate every quantity trade-off for Chen Cheng. She calculated what it would cost to shadow the market herself: leaving before dawn and traveling there and back would take at least half a working day each week, and she still did not have Luo Qi's experience judging quality. So she did not take purchasing authority back. Instead, part of the sales bonus was tied to keeping 90-day inventory turnover within a reasonable range, and each week she reviewed only the seven highest-value purchase orders, which had to include the main alternatives and the reason for the chosen quantity.

In the first month, orders of 60 fell noticeably, while orders of 30 and 40 became more common. The wooden-handled cup inventory began to decline. The new arrangement also produced costs immediately. Luo Qi spent about forty extra minutes a week preparing the seven orders, and Chen Cheng spent another twenty minutes reviewing them. More importantly, Luo Qi once ordered only a small quantity of a new cup already scheduled for in-store promotion because he did not want turnover to slow. The stores ran out on the second day of the promotion week. Chen Cheng then defined the turnover measure explicitly as a range rather than 'the faster, the better,' and the review still remained limited to seven orders instead of expanding to every purchase.

Two months later, the wooden-handled cup inventory had fallen to 82, freeing an entire row of warehouse shelving. Sales no longer maintained the earlier 8 percent growth rate, and the average purchase price no longer fell automatically. Luo Qi still chose products in the market, and Chen Cheng still could not see every negotiation. On Thursday afternoon, he placed the week's seven highest-value purchase orders on her desk. At the bottom of the seventh were three quantities: 20, 40, 60. Chen Cheng turned to the last page and saw that the blue pen had circled 40.
concept: The agency model describes a delegated relationship between a principal and an agent. When the agent possesses more professional or frontline information, while the principal and agent do not fully share the same goals, rewards, or exposure to risk, the agent may choose actions that are legal and locally reasonable but more consistent with the agent's own incentives. Those actions may not maximize the principal's overall interest. Monitoring and incentives can reduce this agency cost, but monitoring itself is costly, and new performance measures can create new behavioral distortions.
explanation: The story first shows that delegation itself has value: Luo Qi has a real information advantage, reducing stockouts while improving purchasing prices and product selection. The distortion comes from the combination of information asymmetry and incomplete goal alignment. A sales-based bonus and the discount for buying 60 both favor having more stock available, while the cash tied up in inventory and the warehouse space it uses do not enter his direct reward. Photographic monitoring can show quoted outcomes but cannot reconstruct all rejected alternatives and quantity trade-offs; Chen Cheng following every purchase personally would also impose a clear time cost while giving up Luo Qi's expertise. Once a turnover range and review of seven orders are introduced, the same buyer immediately changes his order quantities, ruling out weak ability or dishonesty. The later episode of ordering too little shows that monitoring and incentives can reduce agency costs, but cannot eliminate them without cost or new distortions.
mapping: Luo Qi consistently reduces stockouts and purchase prices and improves product selection → delegation is based on a genuine professional information advantage, not principal neglect.

The sales bonus rewards sales and availability, while an order of 60 receives a bulk discount, but inventory capital and shelf space are absent from Luo Qi's direct reward → goals and risk exposure are not fully aligned.

Sales rise 8 percent and average purchase prices fall 3 percent while inventory rises from 48 to 137 → the agent's visible performance improves while the principal's broader inventory outcome worsens.

After a turnover range and review of seven orders are added, full-case orders of 60 fall, but documentation cost and one episode of under-ordering appear → incentives and monitoring can reduce the distortion while also creating new agency and management costs.
boundary: The agency model does not assume that agents are necessarily selfish, lazy, or dishonest, and it does not argue for removing delegation; professional information is often precisely the reason to delegate. Bulk purchasing can also be economically sound. The key is whether relevant inventory, risk, and opportunity costs are considered together. More complete monitoring is usually more expensive, and stronger single-target incentives can create new forms of optimization, so governance design normally reduces rather than eliminates agency costs.
reflection: If you cannot, and should not, reconstruct every purchasing decision in full, which outcomes would you put into the incentive system, and where would you use the seven limited reviews?
